classes.label: Apple scab
classes.cause: A fungal infection that survives the winter in fallen leaves and infects new growth during cool, wet spring weather.
classes.favorable_conditions: Cool (15-21 C), wet spring weather with long leaf-wetness periods.
symptoms: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves
Deformed, curled or prematurely dropping leaves
Dark, scabby lesions on fruit and twigs
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where available
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Prune the canopy to improve airflow and sunlight penetration
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base
Apply a dormant copper spray before bud break
treatment: Apply protectant fungicides (captan or mancozeb) from bud break
Use systemic fungicides (myclobutanil) during high-risk wet periods
Repeat applications according to the product label and local extension advice
Remove and destroy heavily infected shoots and fallen leaves
organic_options: Sulfur or copper-based sprays during dormant and early season
Neem oil as a supporting protectant
classes.expert_note: Scab control depends on protecting new leaves before infection; once lesions appear, fungicides only limit further spread.

classes.label: Apple Black rot
classes.cause: A fungal disease that spreads from cankers on branches and mummified fruit left on the tree or ground.
classes.favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather; trees weakened by drought, freeze injury or poor pruning.
symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots with light centres and purple margins
Brown rot spreading through fruit, ending in black mummies
Sunken, cracked cankers on branches
prevention: Prune out dead and cankered wood during dry weather
Remove mummified fruit and fallen debris
Disinfect pruning tools between cuts
Avoid mechanical injuries to bark and fruit
Maintain tree vigour with balanced nutrition and irrigation
treatment: Remove cankers and mummified fruit before spring
Apply captan or thiophanate-methyl during the growing season
Follow a preventive spray schedule from bud break through fruit development
Consult local extension guidance for resistance management
organic_options: Copper sprays during dormancy
Meticulous sanitation is the most important organic control
classes.expert_note: Black rot is managed mainly through sanitation; fungicides cannot cure established cankers.

classes.label: Cedar apple rust
classes.cause: A rust fungus that requires two hosts: apple trees and juniper or cedar trees. Spores travel between them during wet spring weather.
classes.favorable_conditions: Wet spring weather and the presence of juniper/cedar hosts nearby.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface
Raised orange spore structures under leaves
Premature leaf drop and reduced fruit quality
prevention: Remove nearby juniper or cedar trees that carry the fungus
Remove orange, gelatinous galls from junipers in spring
Choose rust-resistant apple varieties
Space trees for good airflow
treatment: Apply myclobutanil or mancozeb from pink bud through early summer
Protect new growth during wet spring periods
Remove infected leaves and fruit where practical
organic_options: Sulfur sprays during the susceptible spring window
Host removal is the most durable organic strategy
classes.expert_note: The disease cannot persist on apple alone; removing the juniper host breaks the life cycle.

classes.label: Rice Bacterialblight
classes.cause: A bacterial disease spread by infected seed, irrigation water, rain splash and clipping of seedling tips.
classes.favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather, standing water, high nitrogen and typhoon or heavy-rain damage.
symptoms: Water-soaked yellow streaks along leaf edges
Lesions turning white or grey with wavy margins
Wilting of seedlings (kresek) and drying of leaves
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and resistant varieties
Treat seed with hot water or a recommended bactericide
Avoid excessive nitrogen; apply balanced fertilizer
Drain fields periodically and avoid clipping seedling tips
Rotate with non-host crops and remove stubble
treatment: There is no direct cure; remove severely infected plants
Apply copper-based bactericides to reduce spread (label permitting)
Improve drainage and stop excessive nitrogen application
Consult local extension for region-specific resistant varieties
organic_options: Pseudomonas-based biocontrol seed treatment
Balanced organic matter and strict field sanitation
classes.expert_note: Bacterial blight is best managed preventively; bactericides have limited effect once symptoms are widespread.

classes.label: Rice Blast
classes.cause: A highly destructive fungal disease spread by airborne spores and infected seed residues.
classes.favorable_conditions: High humidity, prolonged leaf wetness, cool nights, dense planting and excess nitrogen.
symptoms: Spindle or diamond-shaped lesions with grey centres
Brown margins around lesions on leaves
Neck rot that breaks the panicle and causes empty grains
prevention: Grow blast-resistant varieties suited to your region
Treat seed before sowing
Avoid excess nitrogen and dense sowing
Apply silicon and balanced nutrients
Maintain good water management and remove stubble
treatment: Apply tricyclazole, azoxystrobin or isoprothiolane at early symptoms
Protect the neck at the booting and heading stages
Rotate fungicide groups to avoid resistance
Remove and destroy infected residue after harvest
organic_options: Trichoderma seed treatment and silicon amendments
Bacillus-based biocontrol products as part of an integrated plan
classes.expert_note: Neck blast causes the greatest yield loss; time fungicide applications before heading rather than after damage appears.

classes.label: Rice Brownspot
classes.cause: A seed- and residue-borne fungus that is often worse in nutrient-deficient or water-stressed fields.
classes.favorable_conditions: Poor soils, low nitrogen or silicon, drought stress and high humidity.
symptoms: Oval brown spots with a yellow halo
Seedling blight and poor establishment
Discoloured or shrivelled grain
prevention: Use healthy, certified seed and treat it before sowing
Maintain balanced soil fertility, especially nitrogen and silicon
Add organic matter and avoid drought stress
Rotate crops and remove crop residue
treatment: Apply mancozeb, carbendazim or propiconazole when symptoms appear
Correct nutrient deficiencies alongside fungicide use
Repeat only as recommended on the label
organic_options: Trichoderma seed treatment
Compost and silicon-rich amendments to build soil health
classes.expert_note: Brown spot is often a symptom of a nutrient-stressed crop; fixing soil fertility is as important as spraying.

classes.label: Corn Cercospora leaf spot
classes.cause: A residue-borne fungus that survives in maize stubble and spreads during humid weather.
classes.favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather, prolonged dew and continuous maize cropping.
symptoms: Narrow, rectangular grey-tan lesions between leaf veins
Lesions joining to blight large areas of leaf
Reduced photosynthesis and grain fill
prevention: Rotate away from maize for at least one season
Manage residue through tillage or decomposition
Plant resistant hybrids
Avoid continuous maize and improve airflow
treatment: Apply a strobilurin or triazole fungicide if disease begins early
Protect the upper leaves during grain fill
Rotate fungicide modes of action
organic_options: Residue management and crop rotation are the primary tools
Biofungicides as part of an integrated programme
classes.expert_note: This disease is strongly associated with maize-on-maize rotation; rotation is more effective than late spraying.

classes.label: Corn Common rust
classes.cause: Wind-borne rust spores that infect maize leaves when temperatures are moderate and leaves stay wet.
classes.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (16-23 C), high humidity and long dew periods.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules that rupture and release powdery brown spores
Yellowing and early leaf death in severe cases
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids
Sow early to avoid peak rust pressure
Scout fields regularly from the vegetative stage
Avoid excessive nitrogen that produces overly lush growth
treatment: Fungicides are usually economic only on susceptible hybrids or seed crops
Apply azoxystrobin or propiconazole when pustules first appear
Follow label rates and resistance-management guidance
organic_options: Resistant varieties are the most practical organic control
Sulfur or copper-based products have limited efficacy
classes.expert_note: Common rust often arrives late and may not justify spraying in grain maize; focus on resistant hybrids.

classes.label: Corn Northern Leaf Blight
classes.cause: A residue-borne fungus that survives in maize stubble and spreads by wind and rain splash.
classes.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures, extended wet periods and continuous maize cropping.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped tan lesions on leaves
Lesions spreading from lower to upper leaves
Large blighted areas and premature leaf death
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids with appropriate resistance ratings
Rotate maize with a non-host crop
Bury or decompose infected residue
Avoid dense stands and excessive nitrogen
treatment: Apply a strobilurin or triazole fungicide at early symptom or VT stage
Prioritise protection of the upper leaves
Rotate fungicide groups between seasons
organic_options: Rotation and residue management
Resistant hybrids are the foundation of organic control
classes.expert_note: Early infections above the ear leaf cause the largest yield losses; scout from tasselling onward.

classes.label: Grape Black rot
classes.cause: A fungus that overwinters in mummified berries and infected canes and spreads during warm, wet weather.
classes.favorable_conditions: Warm (20-30 C), humid weather with frequent rain during bloom and fruit development.
symptoms: Tan leaf spots with dark borders and black fruiting dots
Brown rot on berries that shrink into black mummies
Cane lesions and weakened vines
prevention: Remove mummified berries and infected canes during pruning
Improve canopy airflow and sunlight exposure
Control weeds and avoid overhead irrigation
Start protectant sprays before bloom
treatment: Apply myclobutanil, mancozeb or captan according to the label
Maintain protection through bloom and early fruit development
Remove infected clusters promptly
Rotate fungicide groups to prevent resistance
organic_options: Copper or sulfur protectants
Strict sanitation and canopy management
classes.expert_note: The fungus survives in mummies, so removing them is essential even if fungicides are used.

classes.label: Grape Esca (Black Measles)
classes.pathogen: A complex of wood-decay fungi (Phaeomoniella, Phaeoacremonium and related species)
classes.cause: Wood-infecting fungi that enter through pruning wounds and slowly colonise the vine's vascular system.
classes.favorable_conditions: Older vines, large pruning wounds, drought stress and wet pruning conditions.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe chlorosis and necrosis between veins
Dark spots (black measles) on berries
Sudden wilting or dieback of shoots (apoplexy)
prevention: Prune in dry weather and protect large wounds
Avoid large cuts and unnecessary vine injuries
Disinfect pruning tools between vines
Remove and burn severely infected wood
Renew trunks from suckers where practical
treatment: There is no reliable chemical cure for Esca
Surgical removal of affected wood can extend vine life
Replace severely affected vines
Protect pruning wounds with a registered dressing
organic_options: Trunk renewal and sanitation are the main organic options
Reduce vine stress through balanced water and nutrition
classes.expert_note: Esca is a chronic wood disease; prevention through pruning hygiene is far more effective than any spray.

classes.label: Grape Leaf blight (Isariopsis Leaf Spot)
classes.cause: A fungal leaf-spot disease that survives in fallen leaves and spreads during warm, humid weather.
classes.favorable_conditions: Warm, humid conditions, dense canopies and poor air circulation.
symptoms: Angular brown lesions between leaf veins
Lesions with yellow halos and dark centres
Premature defoliation and reduced fruit ripening
prevention: Remove and destroy fallen leaves
Open the canopy with pruning for better airflow
Avoid overhead irrigation and excessive nitrogen
Maintain vineyard sanitation through the season
treatment: Apply copper or mancozeb protectant fungicides
Spray from early symptom detection and repeat per label
Combine sprays with canopy management
organic_options: Copper-based protectants
Canopy management and leaf removal
classes.expert_note: Isariopsis is often a late-season disease; preventing early defoliation helps protect fruit quality and vine reserves.
